goals: Retell the stages of Richard Ebright's growth from collector to scientist, in your own words

Discuss what students can learn from his life

slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study The Making of a Scientist, Robert W. Peterson's account of the American scientist Richard Ebright. Please read the chapter in your supplementary reader first; this lesson does not repeat it. The board tests this book through three mark short answers and a six mark long answer on character, theme and values, so we will practise those most.

slides.heading: How to use this lesson
bullets: Read the chapter once in *Footprints without Feet*, straight through.
Use these slides for the stages of Ebright's life, the themes and his qualities.
Explain events **in your own words**; do not memorise lines.
Practise the 3-mark and 6-mark questions most: that is how the board tests this book.

slides.narration: This chapter is non-fiction. Robert W. Peterson tells the true story of Richard Ebright, who grew from a boy collecting butterflies into a scientist with new ideas about how living cells work. We meet Ebright's mother, the researcher Dr Frederick Urquhart, and the friends who worked with him.

slides.heading: The account in six stages
slides.body_md: A scientist is made step by step. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

nodes.label: A lost fair and a new method

visual.alt: Flow of the account in six stages: a boy who collects; a mother who encourages; a book and the tagging; a lost fair and a new method; experiments and the gold spots; college and the cell theory.
visual.caption: The account in six stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The account moves through six stages. A boy collects everything he finds. His mother encourages him. A book leads him to tag monarch butterflies. He loses a science fair and learns a new method. Experiments lead to the discovery about the gold spots. And at college he develops a theory about cells. Keep this map in mind.

slides.heading: Summary 1: a collector and his mother
slides.body_md: As a child, Ebright collected butterflies above all, along with coins, fossils and stones, and wanted to know about everything he found. He was an only child. After his father died while Richard was still young, his mother became his companion and guide. She took him on trips, bought him instruments for close study and encouraged every question.
slides.narration: Richard Ebright was a born collector, especially of butterflies, and he wanted to understand everything he found. He was an only child, and his father died while he was still young. His mother then became his companion and his guide. She took him on outings, bought him equipment for studying things closely, and made sure his questions were taken seriously.

slides.heading: Summary 2: a book and the tagging
slides.body_md: His mother gave him *The Travels of Monarch X*, about the long migration of monarch butterflies. It invited readers to help research by tagging monarchs for Dr Frederick Urquhart of the University of Toronto. Ebright raised and tagged monarchs. In time the tagging became tiresome, but it had turned a hobby into a contribution to science.
slides.narration: A gift from his mother changed everything. The book, The Travels of Monarch X, described how monarch butterflies migrate, and it invited readers to tag monarchs for Dr Frederick Urquhart's research. Ebright began raising and tagging monarchs. The work grew dull after a while, but it had shown him that his hobby could help real science.

slides.heading: Check: the order of events
slides.narration: Your turn. Five stages of Ebright's life are shuffled. Put them in order, from the young collector to the college researcher.

slides.heading: Summary 3: a lost fair and a new method
slides.body_md: In seventh grade Ebright entered a county science fair and won nothing. Studying the winners, he saw that they had carried out real experiments, not just set out displays. He changed his approach. A later project on a disease that killed monarch caterpillars gave no clear answer, but he moved on and tested the idea that viceroys benefit from resembling monarchs.
slides.narration: In seventh grade Ebright entered a county science fair and won nothing. Instead of giving up, he looked at the winners and saw that they had done real experiments rather than displays. So he changed his method. One later project, on a disease that killed monarch caterpillars, gave no clear answer. He simply moved on and tested an idea about viceroys and monarchs.

slides.heading: Summary 4: the gold spots and beyond
slides.body_md: In high school Ebright asked what the small gold spots on a monarch pupa are for. With a classmate he built equipment and showed that the spots produce a hormone the butterfly needs to develop fully. The work won honours, including at an international fair, and a chance to work in a research laboratory. At Harvard he and his room-mate studied the hormone further and proposed a theory about how cells use the instructions in DNA.
slides.narration: In high school Ebright asked a question no one had asked: what are the gold spots on a monarch pupa for? With a classmate he built equipment and found that the spots produce a hormone the butterfly needs to develop fully. This won him honours and laboratory experience. At Harvard he went further, with a new theory about how cells use their DNA.

slides.narration: This table lines up Ebright's projects with what each taught him. Tagging showed that a hobby could serve research. The lost fair taught him to experiment. The failed disease project taught him to keep going. The viceroy project taught him to test an explanation. And the gold spots gave him a real discovery. Use these stages in long answers.

slides.heading: Theme 1: a scientist is made, not born
slides.body_md: Talent grows when it is fed.
columns:
**What Ebright brought**

- endless curiosity
- a sharp, original mind
- persistence after setbacks

**What helped him grow**

- a mother who encouraged without pushing
- a book that linked a hobby to research
- science fairs, a laboratory, collaborators
slides.narration: The central theme is in the title. A scientist is made, not born. Ebright brought curiosity, a sharp mind and persistence. But he also needed help: a mother who encouraged without pushing, a book that linked his hobby to research, and science fairs and laboratories that gave him chances. In answers, show both sides of this partnership.

slides.heading: A web of themes

rows: Collecting, tagging and asking what the gold spots are for.
His mother's trips, equipment, time and the monarch book.
A lost fair and a project with no result lead to better science.
Questions tested by experiment, not displays.
Competing to learn, not only for prizes.

visual.alt: Table of six themes with where each appears: curiosity, encouragement, learning from failure, real science, the right motive, and all-round growth.

slides.narration: Around that idea sit other themes. Curiosity, from collecting to the gold spots. Encouragement, from his mother. Learning from failure, after the lost fair. Real science, which means testing questions by experiment. The right motive, competing to learn rather than for prizes. And all-round growth, in his debating, speaking, canoeing and photography.

slides.narration: Let us sketch Ebright. He is curious, wanting to know about everything he finds. He is persistent, learning from defeat. He is original, asking what the gold spots do. He is well motivated, competing to learn rather than for trophies. And he is well-rounded, with interests far beyond science. Always pair each quality with an episode from the account.

slides.heading: Ebright's mother: a model parent?
columns:
**What she did**

- became his companion after his father's death
- provided trips, equipment and books
- let his interests stay his own

**Questions for discussion**

- Is money needed, or mainly time and attention?
- Where does encouragement end and pressure begin?
- What can teachers do for children without such support?
slides.narration: Ebright's mother is often the subject of long questions. She became his companion, gave him trips, equipment and books, and let his interests remain his own. Think about the questions on the right. Does support mainly need money, or time and attention? When does encouragement become pressure? And how can teachers help children who lack such a parent?

slides.heading: How Peterson tells the story
bullets: **Biographical account:** a true life, told by an outside writer.
**Chronological order:** childhood → school → college.
**Cause and effect:** each experience leads to the next.
**Explanation of science:** terms like migration, pupa and hormone made clear for general readers.
**A message for readers:** the qualities that make a scientist.
slides.narration: How does Peterson tell the story? It is a biographical account, a true life told by an outside writer. He follows time order, from childhood to college. He shows cause and effect, each experience leading to the next. He explains scientific ideas simply for ordinary readers. And he ends with a message about the qualities that make a scientist.

slides.heading: Cause and effect: SOYL's own examples
slides.body_md: Practise tracing how one step leads to the next, as Peterson does. These sentences are SOYL's own, not from the chapter:
bullets: *A torn kite made her wonder how kites fly; a library book led to a model glider; the glider won a district prize.* — a chain of cause and effect
*He lost the quiz by one point, read every evening that winter, and won the next year.* — failure as a turning point
*Her grandmother gave her a magnifying glass, and the garden became a laboratory.* — encouragement opening a door
slides.narration: Here are three examples of our own. A torn kite leads to a book, then a glider, then a prize: a chain of cause and effect. A boy loses a quiz, studies all winter and wins the next year: failure as a turning point. A gift of a magnifying glass turns a garden into a laboratory: encouragement opening a door. Find the same patterns in Ebright's story.

slides.narration: These words will help you write about the chapter. A monarch is a large orange and black butterfly that migrates. Migration is seasonal travel. A pupa is the stage between caterpillar and adult. A hormone is a chemical messenger in the body. Mimicry means one species looking like another. Tagging marks animals to track them. And persistence means carrying on despite difficulty.

sections.heading: 1. About the text and the author
sections.body_md:
**Read the chapter itself in your supplementary reader, *Footprints without Feet* (NCERT).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the text.

**Robert W. Peterson** wrote this biographical account of **Richard H. Ebright**, an American scientist. It follows Ebright from his childhood as a collector of butterflies to his research at Harvard, and asks what qualities make a scientist.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL's words)
sections.body_md:
**The collector.** Ebright collected butterflies above all, as well as coins, fossils and stones, and wanted to understand each find.

**His mother.** An only child whose father died while he was young, he was guided by his mother, who gave him trips, equipment and encouragement.

**The book and the tagging.** Her gift, *The Travels of Monarch X*, invited readers to tag monarchs for Dr Frederick Urquhart's migration research. Ebright raised and tagged monarchs until the work grew tiresome.

**The lost fair.** In seventh grade he won nothing at a county science fair and learnt that winners did real experiments. A project on a caterpillar disease gave no clear result; another tested why viceroys resemble monarchs.

**The gold spots.** In high school he and a classmate showed that the gold spots on a monarch pupa produce a hormone needed for full development. The work brought honours and laboratory experience.

**College.** At Harvard he and his room-mate studied the hormone and proposed a theory about how cells use the instructions in DNA.

sections.body_md:
- **Curiosity:** the engine of his work.
- **Encouragement:** his mother's support.
- **Learning from failure:** the lost fair and the failed project.
- **Real science:** experiments, not displays.
- **The right motive:** competing to learn.
- **All-round growth:** wide interests beyond science.

**Message:** a scientist is made by curiosity, support and persistence working together.

sections.heading: 8. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**How this book is examined:** the board sets 3-mark short answers (40–50 words; two of three) and a 6-mark long answer (100–120 words) from *Footprints without Feet*, on character, theme and values. It does not set extracts from this book. SOYL chapter tests add commentary passages only as extra practice.

**Short answers (3 marks):** point + evidence + explanation.

**Long answers (6 marks):** a clear stand; three points with evidence in your own words; a link to a theme or value; a one-line conclusion. Extrapolation tasks (Ebright's diary, a letter to Dr Urquhart, a speech) must stay consistent with the account.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** *Footprints without Feet* is tested through 3-mark short answers (40–50 words) and a 6-mark long answer (100–120 words) on character, theme and values (CBSE 2026-27, Section C). No extracts are set from this book.

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant events, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view on character, theme or value), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Saying Ebright won his first science fair: he lost, and learnt from it.
2. Saying the gold spots produce a poison or a colour: they produce a hormone needed for full development.
3. Mixing up who led the tagging research: Dr Frederick Urquhart.
4. Treating his mother as pushy: she encouraged without pressure.
5. Quoting lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the chapter in your supplementary reader, *Footprints without Feet*.

questions.passage_md: Richard Ebright's story begins with a boy who could not stop collecting. Coins, fossils, stones and, above all, butterflies filled his days, and he wanted to know everything about each find. He was an only child, and after his father died when Richard was still in primary school, his mother became his closest companion and his most important teacher. She took him on trips, filled the house with instruments for looking closely at the world, and made sure his questions never went unanswered. Peterson's account makes clear that the scientist was not born ready-made. He was shaped, day by day, by an eager mind and a parent who fed it.

options.text_md: *The Invisible Man*
*The Butterfly Atlas*
*A Brief History of Time*
*The Travels of Monarch X*

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** *The Travels of Monarch X*. She gave him *The Travels of Monarch X*.

questions.stem_md: Why did Ebright lose at the county science fair in seventh grade, according to his own later realisation?

options.text_md: He had made a display instead of doing a real experiment.
He arrived late for the judging.
His project was about the wrong subject.
The judges were unfair to younger students.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** He had made a display instead of doing a real experiment. The winners had experimented; he had only displayed.

questions.stem_md: What did Ebright show the gold spots on a monarch pupa produce?

options.text_md: a poison that keeps birds away
a colour that attracts mates
a hormone needed for full development
a scent that guides migration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a hormone needed for full development. They produce a hormone the butterfly needs to develop fully.

questions.stem_md: According to the theory Ebright tested, why might viceroy butterflies benefit from looking like monarchs?

options.text_md: Monarchs share their food with viceroys.
Looking alike helps them migrate together.
Birds avoid monarchs, so they may avoid viceroys too.
Monarchs protect viceroys from insects.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Birds avoid monarchs, so they may avoid viceroys too. Birds dislike the taste of monarchs; resemblance protects viceroys.

questions.stem_md: What drove Ebright to keep entering science fairs after his first defeat?

options.text_md: a wish to learn and do real science
a need for prize money
his teacher’s threats
jealousy of his classmates

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a wish to learn and do real science. He competed for learning and good work.

questions.stem_md: Which message does *The Making of a Scientist* most strongly convey?

options.text_md: Scientists are born, not made.
Hobbies distract children from real study.
Winning prizes is the main aim of science.
Curiosity, support and persistence together build achievement.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Curiosity, support and persistence together build achievement. Ebright’s success grew from curiosity, his mother’s support and steady effort.

questions.stem_md: A student’s first robotics entry loses at a school fair. Which response follows Ebright’s example?

options.text_md: never entering a fair again
studying what the winners did and building a real test into next year’s project
complaining that the judges were biased
copying a winning project exactly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** studying what the winners did and building a real test into next year’s project. Ebright learnt from the winners and changed his method.

questions.stem_md: Which word best describes Ebright’s mother in the account?

options.text_md: strict
indifferent
encouraging
anxious

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** encouraging. She supported his interests with books, trips and equipment.

questions.stem_md: What did Ebright’s college research lead to?

options.text_md: a cure for a butterfly disease
a new theory about how cells use the instructions in their DNA
a map of monarch migration routes
a new kind of camera

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a new theory about how cells use the instructions in their DNA. He and his room-mate proposed a theory about how cells use the instructions in DNA.

questions.stem_md: How is *The Making of a Scientist* mainly organised?

options.text_md: as a series of letters
as a dialogue between Ebright and his mother
as a diary kept by Ebright
as a chronological account from childhood to college

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** as a chronological account from childhood to college. Peterson follows Ebright’s life in time order, stage by stage.

questions.stem_md: Ebright tagged monarch butterflies for the research of Dr Frederick ___.
questions.solution_md: He tagged them for Dr Frederick **Urquhart**.

questions.stem_md: The butterflies at the heart of Ebright’s early research were ___ butterflies.
questions.solution_md: Most of his work was on **monarch** butterflies.

questions.stem_md: Ebright studied the gold ___ on the monarch ___.
questions.solution_md: He studied the gold **spots** on the monarch **pupa**.

questions.stem_md: Ebright later studied at ___ University, where he continued his research.
questions.solution_md: He went to **Harvard**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ebright’s mother played a major part in his development as a scientist.

**Reason (R):** She encouraged his interests with trips, equipment and the book on monarch migration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ebright lost at the county science fair in seventh grade.

**Reason (R):** Ebright’s project at that fair was a careful experiment on the gold spots.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the gold-spot work came later; at that fair he had only a display.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ebright began tagging monarch butterflies.

**Reason (R):** Ebright enjoyed debating and public speaking.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but his debating does not explain the tagging, which answered the book’s invitation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ebright gave up science after his project on the caterpillar disease failed.

**Reason (R):** Ebright’s project on the disease killing monarch caterpillars did not give a clear result.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: he moved on to new projects. R is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Richard Ebright’s father guided his science projects throughout high school.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** His father died when he was young; his mother guided him.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Ebright eventually found tagging monarch butterflies tedious.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The repetitive work grew dull, and he turned to new questions.

questions.stem_md: True or false: according to Peterson, Ebright competed in science fairs only to win prizes.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** He competed to learn and to do good work.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Ebright’s gold-spot research earned him the chance to work in a research laboratory while still at school.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** His success led to laboratory work as a student.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these stages of Richard Ebright’s life in the order in which they happen.

options.text_md: His mother gives him *The Travels of Monarch X*.
At college he develops a theory about how cells use DNA.
He discovers what the gold spots on the pupa produce.
Ebright collects butterflies as a young child.
He loses at a county science fair in seventh grade.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (a) → (e) → (c) → (b). Collecting → the book → the lost fair → the gold spots → college research.
